content.title: About
content.content: Artichoke (Cynara cardunculus var. scolymus) is the edible flower bud of a thistle-like plant native to the Mediterranean. It has layers of tough, overlapping green leaves (bracts) around a tender, fleshy heart. Artichokes have a nutty, slightly sweet, earthy flavor and are eaten steamed, boiled, roasted, grilled, or from jars and cans.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The artichoke is a flower bud that would bloom into a large purple flower if left to mature.
Only the fleshy base of the leaves and the heart are eaten, while the fuzzy choke inside is removed.
A compound called cynarin can make foods eaten right after artichoke taste slightly sweeter.
Artichokes belong to the daisy family, along with sunflowers and thistles.
Artichokes have been eaten in the Mediterranean region for thousands of years.

items.title: Rich in dietary fiber
items.content: Artichokes are a good source of fiber, including inulin, a prebiotic fiber that feeds beneficial gut bacteria.

items.title: Provides folate and vitamin K
items.content: These vitamins support cell function and normal blood clotting.

items.title: Provides vitamin C and magnesium
items.content: These nutrients support the immune system and muscle function.

items.title: Contains polyphenols
items.content: Artichokes contain antioxidant compounds such as cynarin and chlorogenic acid.

items.title: Low in calories
items.content: Artichokes are low in calories and filling.

items.title: Allergic reactions
items.content: People allergic to plants in the daisy family, such as ragweed or chamomile, may react to artichokes.

items.title: Gallbladder and bile ducts
items.content: Artichoke stimulates bile flow, so people with gallstones or bile duct problems should consult a healthcare professional, especially before using artichoke extracts.

items.title: Gas and bloating
items.content: The inulin in artichokes may cause gas or bloating in sensitive individuals.

items.title: Sodium in canned artichokes
items.content: Canned and jarred artichokes can be high in added salt, so rinse them and check labels.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Whole artichokes are steamed or boiled until the leaves pull off easily, then the base of each leaf is scraped with the teeth and the heart is eaten, often dipped in sauce. Trimmed hearts can be roasted, grilled, sautéed, or added to salads, pizzas, pasta, and dips. Rub cut surfaces with lemon to prevent browning.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store fresh, unwashed artichokes in the refrigerator in a bag, where they keep for about five to seven days. Cooked artichokes should be refrigerated in an airtight container and eaten within three to five days. Artichoke hearts can also be frozen.

content.title: About
content.content: Savoy cabbage is a variety of Brassica oleracea with crinkly, light‑green leaves. When cooked it retains a mild, slightly sweet flavor and a tender texture. It is commonly used in side dishes, soups, and stews.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Savoy cabbage originates from the Mediterranean region but is now cultivated worldwide.
Its leaves have distinctive wavy margins that set it apart from regular green cabbage.
Savoy cabbage is a staple in many Eastern European dishes, such as Polish bigos.
Cooking preserves most of its B‑vitamins and vitamin C if not overcooked.
It is rich in antioxidants like quercetin.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: Cooked savoy cabbage provides a good amount of vitamin C, which supports the immune system and collagen synthesis.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: The fiber content promotes healthy bowel movements and feeds beneficial gut bacteria.

items.title: Low in calories
items.content: A serving of cooked savoy cabbage contains about 25 kcal, making it an excellent choice for weight‑management diets.

items.title: Antioxidant properties
items.content: Phytochemicals such as glucosinolates help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Cardiovascular support
items.content: Potassium and magnesium in cabbage contribute to normal blood pressure regulation.

items.title: Gas formation
items.content: Cabbage contains raffinose, which can cause gas and bloating in sensitive individuals.

items.title: Thyroid interaction
items.content: Glucosinolates may affect thyroid function when consumed in large amounts raw; cooking reduces this risk.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Rarely, some people may experience an allergic reaction to cabbage.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Cooked savoy cabbage can be served as a side dish, added to soups, stews, salads, or baked with cheese. It pairs well with carrots, onions, and spices such as caraway or dill.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cooked cabbage in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. For longer storage, freeze it (after cooling) in a freezer‑safe bag for up to 2 months.

content.title: About
content.content: Glazed cooked carrots are boiled carrot pieces coated with a sweet glaze made from sugar, butter, and sometimes spices. They retain a bright orange color and a tender texture, making them a popular side dish.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Glazed carrots are a classic garnish in many European and American meals.
The sugar in the glaze helps lock in the carrot’s natural sweetness and vivid color.
The "glazed carrots" style became popular in the United States in the early 20th century as a kid‑friendly vegetable preparation.
Carrots are rich in beta‑carotene, which the body converts to vitamin A.
Glazing can be done with honey, maple syrup, or orange juice for a flavor twist.

items.title: High in beta‑carotene
items.content: Beta‑carotene supports vision, immune function, and skin health.

items.title: Source of vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C provides antioxidant protection and aids iron absorption.

items.title: Low in calories
items.content: A typical serving (≈100 g) contains about 70 kcal, making it diet‑friendly.

items.title: Contains dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber promotes healthy digestion and a feeling of fullness.

items.title: Provides potassium
items.content: Potassium helps maintain normal blood pressure.

items.title: Added sugar
items.content: The glaze adds simple sugars, so people with diabetes should watch portion size.

items.title: Carrot allergy
items.content: Rare, but some individuals may be allergic to carrots.

items.title: Digestive sensitivity
items.content: Large amounts of fiber can cause gas in sensitive individuals.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve glazed carrots warm as a side dish with meat, poultry, or fish. They also work well in salads, vegetable casseroles, or as a festive appetizer.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep cooked glazed carrots in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. Reheat gently in a pan or microwave before serving.

content.title: About
content.content: Chocolate hazelnut spread is a sweet paste made from roasted hazelnuts, cocoa mass, sugar and vegetable oils. It has a creamy texture, a rich chocolate‑nut flavor and is commonly used as a spread on bread, pancakes, in desserts and baked goods.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The spread originated in Italy in the 1940s under the name “Nutella” and later became popular worldwide.
Hazelnuts, the main ingredient, contain more monounsaturated fats than most other nuts.
Cocoa mass usually makes up 10‑15 % of the product, giving it a distinct chocolate aroma.
The spread is often used as a quick source of energy for athletes and children.
Some markets offer versions without added palm oil.

items.title: Rich in vitamin E
items.content: Hazelnuts provide vitamin E, a powerful antioxidant that supports skin health.

items.title: Contains healthy monounsaturated fats
items.content: Monounsaturated fatty acids help maintain normal cholesterol levels.

items.title: Source of magnesium
items.content: Magnesium supports muscle and nerve function as well as protein synthesis.

items.title: Contains iron
items.content: Iron from hazelnuts contributes to normal hemoglobin levels.

items.title: Antioxidant compounds
items.content: Cocoa mass and phenolic compounds in hazelnuts have antioxidant activity.

items.title: Tree nut allergy
items.content: Hazelnuts are tree nuts and can trigger allergic reactions, up to anaphylaxis, in sensitive individuals.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: The spread contains added sugar, so it should be consumed in moderation, especially by people with diabetes.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: One tablespoon provides about 100 kcal, which can contribute to weight gain if eaten excessively.

items.title: Palm oil
items.content: Some versions contain palm oil, which may be a concern for those limiting saturated fat intake.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Spread can be used on bread, toast, pancakes, as a filling for cupcakes and cookies, as a topping for ice cream, or mixed into yogurt for a quick snack.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in a sealed jar in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. After opening, keep refrigerated to preserve freshness and prevent fat oxidation.

content.title: About
content.content: Canned orange slices in syrup are whole orange segments that have been blanched, placed in a sugar‑water syrup, and sealed in glass jars. The product retains the sweet‑tart flavor of fresh oranges with a soft, ready‑to‑eat texture and a long shelf life.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Canning helps preserve vitamin C, although some is lost during heat processing.
The syrup often contains a touch of citric acid to prevent browning of the fruit.
Orange slices in syrup are a traditional ingredient in Eastern European desserts and pastries.
Jars of canned oranges are sometimes used as decorative elements on holiday tables.

items.title: Source of vitamin C
items.content: Even after processing, canned oranges still provide vitamin C, which supports immune function and antioxidant protection.

items.title: Rich in dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber aids normal digestion and helps maintain a feeling of fullness.

items.title: Contains flavonoids
items.content: Flavonoids such as hesperidin have antioxidant properties and may support vascular health.

items.title: Quick source of energy
items.content: The syrup adds simple carbohydrates, making the product a fast‑acting energy source for children and athletes.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Canned oranges contain virtually no fat, fitting well into low‑fat dietary plans.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: The syrup is rich in sugar, so consumption should be moderate, especially for people with diabetes or weight concerns.

items.title: Citrus allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to oranges.

items.title: Acidity
items.content: The natural acidity can irritate a sensitive stomach or enamel.

items.title: Preservatives
items.content: Certain brands may add preservatives (e.g., potassium sorbate) that can cause reactions in sensitive persons.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Canned orange slices can be enjoyed straight from the jar, added to yogurt, cottage cheese, salads, baked goods, ice cream, or used in sauces for meat dishes. Shake the jar before opening and drain excess syrup if a less sweet result is desired.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the unopened jar in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. After opening, keep it refrigerated and consume within 1–2 weeks. Discard the product if mold, off‑odors, or discoloration appear.

content.title: About
content.content: Poppy seed dressing is a thick sauce made from ground poppy seeds, vegetable oil, vinegar, and spices. It has a delicate nutty aroma, a mildly sweet flavor, and a characteristic creamy texture. It is used in salads, as a marinade for fish and meat, and as a sauce for vegetable dishes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Poppy seeds are rich in linoleic acid, which gives the dressing its distinctive scent.
Traditional recipes come from Eastern European cuisines, especially Polish and Russian kitchens.
Apple cider vinegar is often used in the original recipe to highlight the natural sweetness of poppy seeds.
The dressing can be kept in the refrigerator for up to two weeks without losing flavor or texture.
Ground poppy seeds help stabilize the emulsion, preventing separation.

items.title: Rich in healthy fats
items.content: Poppy seed oil contains polyunsaturated fatty acids that support cardiovascular health.

items.title: Source of calcium and magnesium
items.content: Poppy seeds provide minerals that contribute to bone strength and normal muscle function.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Vitamin E and flavonoids in the dressing help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: Fiber from poppy seeds aids regular bowel movements.

items.title: Low in added sugar
items.content: The dressing’s sweetness comes from the natural flavor of poppy seeds, without large amounts of added sugar.

items.title: Poppy allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to poppy seeds.

items.title: High calorie content
items.content: Because of the oil, the dressing is relatively calorie‑dense and should be used in moderation.

items.title: Oxalate content
items.content: Poppy seeds contain oxalates, which can contribute to kidney stone formation in susceptible people.

content.title: How to Use
content.content: Drizzle the dressing over salads, add it to marinades for fish, chicken or pork, use as a sauce for roasted vegetables, or serve as a dip with bread and crackers.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the dressing in an airtight container in the refrigerator at 2‑4 °C. Stir before each use if separation occurs. Discard if it develops an off‑odor or changes color.

content.title: About
content.content: Rice paper are thin sheets made from rice flour, water and sometimes starch. Traditionally used in Southeast Asian cuisines for rolls, spring rolls and wraps, the paper has a soft, slightly elastic texture and a neutral taste that lets the filling shine.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Rice paper production began in Vietnam in the early 1920s.
It can be either translucent or milky‑white depending on the ratio of rice flour to starch.
Unlike traditional rice noodles, the sheets do not require cooking – a quick soak in warm water for 10–20 seconds is enough.
Some varieties include seaweed extracts, giving the paper a subtle marine aroma.
Crisped rice paper chips are a popular snack after a brief fry.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Rice paper contains virtually no fat, making it suitable for low‑calorie diets.

items.title: Rich source of complex carbs
items.content: The main component is complex carbohydrates that provide a steady release of energy.

items.title: Gluten‑free
items.content: Made from pure rice flour, it is safe for people with celiac disease.

items.title: Contains small amounts of B‑vitamins
items.content: Rice flour retains modest levels of thiamine and niacin, supporting metabolism.

items.title: Easy to digest
items.content: The thin structure aids digestion, especially in light dishes.

items.title: Rice allergy
items.content: A small number of individuals may experience an allergic reaction to rice flour.

items.title: Sodium content in processed sheets
items.content: Some ready‑made sheets are salted; people monitoring sodium intake should check the label.

items.title: Microbial contamination
items.content: Improper storage can allow mold growth; keep the product in proper conditions.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Soak the sheets in warm water for 10–20 seconds until pliable, then wrap fresh vegetables, seafood, meat or tofu. They can be quickly pan‑fried for a crisp edge or baked in the oven. As a snack, cut the sheets into strips and fry them to make rice chips.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store rice paper in an airtight package in a cool, dry place away from direct light. For longer shelf life keep it in the refrigerator, where it stays flexible for up to 6 months. Discard any sheets that develop a moldy smell or discoloration.
